Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

The **director general of the Foreign Service** is the designated manager of the [United States Foreign Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Foreign_Service "United States Foreign Service").

The director general is a current or former [Foreign Service officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Service_officer "Foreign Service officer"), appointed by the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), with the advice and consent of the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_General_of_the_Foreign_Service#cite_note-LII-2) Since November 23, 1975, under a departmental administrative action, the director general has concurrently held the title of Director of the [Bureau of Global Talent Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Global_Talent_Management "Bureau of Global Talent Management").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_General_of_the_Foreign_Service#cite_note-Historian-3) As the head of the human resources bureau, the director general holds a rank equivalent to an [assistant secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Assistant_Secretary_of_State "United States Assistant Secretary of State") and reports to the [under secretary of state for management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_State_for_Management "Under Secretary of State for Management").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_General_of_the_Foreign_Service#cite_note-Historian-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_General_of_the_Foreign_Service#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_General_of_the_Foreign_Service#cite_note-5)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Director_General_of_the_Foreign_Service&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") created the position of Director General of the Foreign Service through the [Foreign Service Act of 1946](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Foreign_Service#Foreign_Service_Act_of_1946 "United States Foreign Service"). Between 1946 and 1980, the [secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") designated the director general.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_General_of_the_Foreign_Service#cite_note-Historian-3)

The [Foreign Service Act of 1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Foreign_Service#Foreign_Service_Act_of_1980 "United States Foreign Service") made the position a [presidential appointee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_positions_filled_by_presidential_appointment_with_Senate_confirmation "List of positions filled by presidential appointment with Senate confirmation").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_General_of_the_Foreign_Service#cite_note-Historian-3)

After 1986, the director general became responsible for all personnel aspects of the Foreign Service and the [civil service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_service_(United_States) "Civil service (United States)") at the [State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), including advertising, examination, appointment, job assignments worldwide, disciplinary actions, and promotions to the [Senior Foreign Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senior_Foreign_Service "Senior Foreign Service").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_General_of_the_Foreign_Service#cite_note-ADST-6)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Person conducting diplomacy with another entity

For other uses, see [Diplomat (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomat_(disambiguation) "Diplomat (disambiguation)").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Charles_Maurice_de_Talleyrand-P%C3%A9rigord_by_Fran%C3%A7ois_G%C3%A9rard%2C_1808.jpg/250px-Charles_Maurice_de_Talleyrand-P%C3%A9rigord_by_Fran%C3%A7ois_G%C3%A9rard%2C_1808.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_Maurice_de_Talleyrand-P%C3%A9rigord_by_Fran%C3%A7ois_G%C3%A9rard,_1808.jpg)

_[Portrait of Talleyrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait\_of\_Talleyrand "Portrait of Talleyrand")_ by [François Gérard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_G%C3%A9rard "François Gérard"), 1808. French statesman and [Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_of_the_French "Emperor of the French")[Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon")'s chief diplomat [Charles Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Maurice_de_Talleyrand-P%C3%A9rigord "Charles Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord") (1754–1838) is widely considered one of the most skilled diplomats of all time.

A **diplomat** (from [Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): δίπλωμα, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"):_diploma_) is a person appointed by a [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_(polity) "State (polity)"), [intergovernmental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organization "International organization"), or [nongovernmental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organization "Non-governmental organization") institution to conduct [diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomacy "Diplomacy") with one or more other states or [international organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organization "International organization").

The main functions of diplomats are representation and protection of the interests and nationals of the sending state; initiation and facilitation of strategic agreements, treaties and conventions; and promotion of information, trade and commerce, technology, and friendly relations. Seasoned diplomats of international repute are used in international organizations (for example, the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"), the world's largest diplomatic forum) as well as multinational companies for their experience in management and [negotiating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negotiation "Negotiation") skills. Diplomats are members of foreign services and diplomatic corps of various nations of the world.

The sending state is required to get the consent of the receiving state for a person proposed to serve in key diplomatic positions such as an [ambassador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador "Ambassador"), also referred to as the head of the mission. The receiving state of the proposed diplomat may accept the diplomat or refuse to accept the diplomat without having to provide reasons for its refusal or acceptance of the person. While the head of the mission or any member of the diplomatic staff is already on duty in the receiving state, the receiving state may still decide at anytime that the person is no longer wanted in the state and is considered [persona non grata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persona_non_grata "Persona non grata"). When this happens, the sending state may discharge the person.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomat#cite_note-1)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Government bodies and personnel who communicate with the governments of other countries

Not to be confused with [Diplomatic corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_corps "Diplomatic corps").

**Diplomatic service** (or **foreign service**) is the body of [diplomats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomat "Diplomat") and [foreign policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_policy "Foreign policy") officers maintained by the government of a country to communicate with the governments of other countries. Diplomatic personnel obtain [diplomatic immunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_immunity "Diplomatic immunity") when they are accredited to other countries. Diplomatic services are often part of the larger [civil service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_service "Civil service") and sometimes a constituent part of the [foreign ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs "Ministry of Foreign Affairs").

Some intergovernmental organizations, such as the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"), and some international non-state organizations, such as the [Sovereign Military Order of Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_Military_Order_of_Malta "Sovereign Military Order of Malta"), may also retain diplomatic services in other jurisdictions. For non-state organizations, the reciprocation of diplomatic recognition by other jurisdictions is difficult, as diplomacy tends to establish the concept of recognition upon an assumed sovereignty over geographical territory; the SMOM, in this case, receives diplomats at its headquarters in Rome, as all permanent missions to the SMOM are jointly accredited as permanent missions to the Holy See. In relation, many more non-state international organizations, such as the [IFRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_Red_Cross_and_Red_Crescent_Societies "International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies")/[ICRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Committee_of_the_Red_Cross "International Committee of the Red Cross"), maintain permanent [non-voting observer status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observer_status "Observer status") to intergovernmental bodies such as the [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly"), appointing individual representatives to the observer office.

September 10, 2026

(_As prepared for delivery_):

Good afternoon.

My wife, Harriet, and I would like to welcome you all to the U.S. Embassy as we gather to remember a significant and sobering milestone: 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the United States.

That fateful day remains not only in our memories as if it were yesterday, but also in our hearts. I’m sure everyone in this room would say the same.

Indeed, the world has not been the same since. 9/11 changed everything from how we live, to how we travel, to how our countries interact with each other.

But the most profound impacts were not societal or political.

They were personal.

Nearly 3,000 people died in the attacks on New York, Washington D.C., and Shanksville, Pennsylvania – including 67 UK citizens.

The names, faces, and voices of those brave souls – many of which survive in the recordings left by passengers on the planes and in the towers– will remain with us forever.

That includes the heroes on board United Airlines Flight 93, who with the famous line “let’s roll,” fought to regain control of the plane and divert it from its target.

Those words would become a rallying cry for the proponents of freedom.

But to many, those fallen heroes were parents, partners, friends, and co-workers. The son of a dear friend of ours was in the second tower and miraculously survived the attack – but I know that is not everyone’s story.

So on this 25 th anniversary, we remember not only those who perished, but those who survived them: the children, family, and friends of the victims.

We cannot imagine your suffering, nor how your world was transformed by this single day; but we want you to know that our devotion to you and your loved ones has not wavered one bit in the 25 years since.

We also remember the thousands who were serving on the frontlines after 9/11: the first responders, law enforcement officers, intelligence services, armed forces, and diplomatic corps.

That includes many of you here who worked to clear backlogs, implement new regulations, and intercept new threats.

You showed unimaginable bravery to keep the world turning when it felt like all had stopped – and your dedication to service continues to inspire us today.

Because while 9/11 brought heartache and hurt; it also revealed humanity and hope.

In the wake of the attacks, thousands of selfless citizens signed up to serve their country – in the military, the fire services, here in the State Department, the broader U.S. government, and beyond – motivated by a love for their country and a desire to help their countrymen however they could.

Around the world, private companies showed unflinching generosity in providing financial assistance and support to keep the global economy moving – even taking on each other’s clients without regard to their own balance sheets or profits.

That was only the beginning of the response: because in the weeks and months that followed 9/11, a new chapter was added to the world’s most historic partnership.

As America grieved, the people of the UK rallied to stand beside us in sympathy and solidarity.

The American national anthem played at Buckingham Palace at the order of Her Late Majesty Queen Elizabeth II: the first time another country’s anthem had been performed during the Changing of the Guard.

Days later, the UK’s Prime Minister, Tony Blair, travelled to Washington D.C. to attend the joint session of Congress and stand shoulder-to-shoulder with President Bush and the American people.

Away from the public eye, our military and intelligence communities began to work together on a level unseen in international relations: sharing information, conducting joint operations, and disrupting threats in the weeks and months after 9/11.

That cooperation saved countless lives – and it continues to save lives today.

We must always remember the painful lessons 9/11 taught us.

Because despite our disagreements and debates, the U.S.-UK partnership has kept us safe for centuries: helping us overcome threats from Nazi tyranny to communist ideology to terrorist insurgency.

Each time, our adversaries have underestimated us; each time, we have risen to the challenge.

Even today, officials across our two countries know that when things get really serious – when lives are at stake – the first people we call are each other. And we call knowing the other side will answer.

25 years ago, that solidarity was on full display.

In one of America’s darkest hours, the UK – a nation attuned to grief and terror – rose as one to stand

(_As prepared for delivery_):

Good evening everyone!

Let me be the _first_ to wish you a very Happy Fourth of July!

On behalf of President Trump,my wife, Harriet,our entire family,and the United States Mission to the United Kingdom,I’d like to welcome you to this historic celebration of American independence.

We are gathered to celebrate a special and significant milestone for America:250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence–our semiquincentennial.

And in saying that word,the hardest part of my night is now over.

As we celebrate this Fourth of July,we are reminded where our story started:with 56 brave men who, in signing a declaration to the King of England,put their lives at risk to pledge,as the Declaration of Independence concludes,“our lives, our fortunes, and our sacred honor.”

They paid the cost:17 signers had their homes destroyed or confiscated.

But they did it to build a new country based on the idea of freedom.

Which is why, on this 250th Fourth of July, we should also be reminded, and frankly incredibly proud, of how far we have come.

What started as a few dispersed colonies fighting famine, disease,and the world’s most powerful empire,has since become the most prosperous nation on earth.

An experiment in democracy has proven itself to be an effective form of government,giving people freedom and opportunity one could have only dreamed of in 1776.

And from the redwoods of California to the delta of Arkansas…from the bayous of Louisiana to the skyscrapers of New York…from the deserts of Arizona to the monuments of Washington, DC…a nation as vast and varied as ours has created and maintained our distinct national identity.

That variety is on full display tonight,as we showcase the best of all 50 states in this“Grand American Jubilee.”

From _my_ home state, I am proud to welcome the fantastic University of Arkansas’Razorback marching band that you heard on your way in,and the Episcopal Collegiate School steel band, “The Steelcats,”that will play when you depart later this evening.

We are also delighted to welcome tonight one of the United States’greatest performing artists–a man whose iconic sound has taken him from New Orleans to Nashville and then around the world multiple times over.

I am speaking, of course, about the legendary Tim McGraw, who we can’t wait to hear from shortly.

Tonight is truly an all-American celebration– and I’d like to thank everyone who has helped make it happen.

To Claire Messano and the team from Half Shell… to the embassy staff and volunteers…to our fantastic and generous sponsors…and especially to my wife,Harriet,for the countless hours spent planning this wonderful celebration.

Thank you so very much.

Standing here now I am feeling, truly,“proud to be an American.”

But while today is a celebration of the United States–I hope it is not just the Americans who feel pride in this special milestone.

Because America’s story is, in truth, inseparable from the United Kingdom’s.The same country we declared independence from 250 years ago has been, and remains,our closest ally today.

The same country that gave us ideas from the rights of man to the rule of law–ideas that are written into our founding documents and that President Trump so eloquently called,_“the richest inheritance one nation has ever given to another.”_

Shortly after independence, in 1785–when our first ambassador to Great Britain and later second president,John Adams, met King George III–he said:

“I shall esteem myself the happiest of men, if I can… restore‘the old good nature and the old good humour’between People who, though separated by an Ocean…have the same language, a similar religion and a kindred blood.”

Well,John Adams would be proud to see this gathering today– and to see the “old good humour” restored between our nations.

As we celebrate America’s 250th birthday this week, let us reflect on our accomplishments and achievements.

One can only dream of what the next 250 years will bring to our extraordinary country, the world, and this special relationship.

So please join me in raising a glass to the people of the United States and the United Kingdom as we toast to the continued health, success, and happiness of America and all our allies…and may freedom always ring.

Thank you and please enjoy the evening!

A career member of the Senior Foreign Service, Faris Y. Asad arrived in August 2026 as Deputy Chief of Mission at the U.S. Embassy in Accra, Ghana. Mr. Asad most recently served as Director of North African Affairs in the Bureau of Near Eastern Affairs in Washington, D.C.

# Principal Officers and Chiefs of Mission

## NOTE TO READERS

Updates to the Principal Officers and Chiefs of Mission database are currently suspended. For information about the Department’s current and recent leadership, we recommend visiting the Department of State homepage’s [Biographies of Senior Officials](https://www.state.gov/biographies-list/) and [List of U.S. Ambassadors](https://www.state.gov/resources-bureau-of-global-talent-management/#ambassadors).

Notice posted on January 12, 2024.   
 Last updated March 14, 2024.

*   [All Principal Officers and Chiefs of Mission, Listed by Name](https://history.state.gov/departmenthistory/people/by-name)
*   [All Principal Officers and Chiefs of Mission, Listed by Year](https://history.state.gov/departmenthistory/people/by-year)
*   [Principal Officers, Listed By Title](https://history.state.gov/departmenthistory/people/principalofficers)
*   [Chiefs of Mission, Listed by Country](https://history.state.gov/departmenthistory/people/chiefsofmission/by-country)
*   [Chiefs of Mission, Listed By International Organization](https://history.state.gov/departmenthistory/people/chiefsofmission/by-organization)

## Introduction

This online resource continues a long tradition in the U.S. Department of State of making retrospective data about principal officers and chiefs of mission available to the public. The 1873 edition of the _Register of the Department of State_ presented the names of all American diplomatic representatives who had served in each country with which the United States had relations from 1789 to 1873. The 1937 edition of the _Register_ presented a cumulative listing of all of the principal officers of the Department of State from 1789 to 1936. The _Biographic Register_ (as the _Register of the United States_ was renamed) of 1957 presented an updated listing of principal diplomatic agents of the United States from 1789 to 1956, together with a listing of the dates of service of Presidents of the United States and Secretaries of State. In 1973, the Department of State issued [United States Chiefs of Mission, 1778−1973](https://hdl.handle.net/2027/txu.059172130110486), which presented in tabular format a comprehensive historical listing of all United States Ambassadors, Ministers, Ministers Resident, Chargés d’Affaires pro tempore, and diplomatic agents. The publication also included a listing of principal officers of the Department. The Department published [United States Chiefs of Mission, 1973−1974 (Supplement)](https://www.hathitrust.org/usdocs_registry/catalog/7a062c55-8462-45a0-a679-4cce574a9c40) in 1975 with addenda and corrigenda to the 1973 edition. [United States Chiefs of Mission, 1778−1982](https://hdl.handle.net/2027/pur1.32754077529729) brought the full text to its second edition.

[Principal Officers of the Department of State and United States Chiefs of Mission, 1778−1986](https://www.hathitrust.org/usdocs_registry/catalog/d1433295-fdbd-4457-a683-bd877633aaa0) issued by the Department of State in 1986, presented expanded listings based on previous Department publications and additional research and definition. Corrections were made to earlier listings, and information on major executive officers of the Department of State was greatly increased and rearranged. A revised edition, [Principal Officers of the Department of State and United States Chiefs of Mission, 1778−1988](https://www.hathitrust.org/usdocs_registry/catalog/a0971723-6d86-4d54-8b81-f77b8c584fbd), was issued in 1988. The final print version of this publication was released in 1991, under the title [Principal Officers of the Department of State and United States Chiefs of Mission, 1778−1990](https://hdl.handle.net/2027/pur1.32754062053008). The transfer of this material online has not changed our office’s intent: to document the history of U.S. representation abroad and the chief policymakers in the Department of State. To that end, we have provided a chronological listing of principal officers—essentially all Department officers at the level of Assistant Secretary or above—and Chiefs of Mission. (See below for a discussion of the term, “Chief of Mission.”) These two categories require Presidential or Secretarial designation, and, in some cases, the approval of the Senate. We have made an attempt to comprehensively list all people selected for these positions, even if they were not approved by the Senate, died before taking office, declined the position, or were otherwise unable to serve. For that reason, the pages which list our Chiefs of Mission by country are split into two categories: “Chiefs of Mission” lists those who held the office, and “Other Nominees” lists those who did not.

### Positions Included

This database includes officers of the Department who were Presidential appointees (appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate) and chiefs of bureaus who hold rank equivalent to Assistant Secretary of State. These include: Secretaries, Deputy Secretaries, Under Secretaries, Deputy Under Secretaries, Assistant Secretaries, Counselors, Legal Advisers, Chiefs of Protocol, and certain administrators.

Other positions have, from time to time, been included in the database based on their particular circumstances. The complete lists of heads of the United States Information Agency (USIA), for example, are included. USIA was incorporated into the Department in 1999. Other Chiefs of Mission of particular historical interest have also been included.

### Positions Excluded

This database does _not_ include representatives, personal representatives, or special representatives of the President or Department of State; Chargés d’Affaires or Chargés d’Affaires ad interim (except under certain circumstances); individuals holding diplomatic commissions jointly with other representatives; special agents and other individuals on special missions; high commissioners; Chiefs of Mission in charge of special economic or aid missions; liaison officers; military governors or commanding officers of occupying forces or their political advisers; delegates to international conferences; or consular officers who held only consular commissions.

### What is a Chief of Mission?

According to the [Foreign Affairs Act of 1980 (Public Law 96−465, Section 102(3) (22 U.S.C. 3902))](http://uscode.house.gov/statutes/pl/96/465.pdf), a Chief of Mission is “the principal officer in charge of a diplomatic mission of the United States or of a United States office abroad which is designated by the Secretary of State as diplomatic in nature, including any individual assigned under section 502(c) to be temporarily in charge of such a mission or office.”

The Chief of Mission is often—but not always—an Ambassador. There are currently three classes of diplomatic representation established by the[1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, Article 14](https://2009-2017.state.gov/documents/organization/17843.pdf): ambassador or nuncio (accredited to the Head of State); envoy, minister, or internuncio (accredited to the Head of State); and chargé d’affaires (accredited to the Minister of Foreign Affairs). These classes have a much longer lineage. Although not a signatory, the United States followed Annex 17 to the Congress Treaty of Vienna (March 19, 1815), which established rank and precedence of diplomatic agents (Ambassadors, Envoys, and Chargés d’Affaires). The Proces-Verbal of the Conference of Aix-la-Chapelle (November 9, 1818), recognized Ministers Resident as an intermediate class between Ministers and Chargés d’Affaires.

The United States first used the rank of Ambassador in 1893, when[Thomas F. Bayard](https://history.state.gov/departmenthistory/people/bayard-thomas-francis) was appointed Ambassador to Great Britain on March 30 of that year.

A “Chargé d’Affaires ad interim” refers to a diplomat temporarily acting for an absent Chief of Mission. This database tracks all Chargés d’Affaires and Chargés d’Affaires ad interim who served (1) for a continuous period of 12 months or more, (2) at the establishment or ending of diplomatic relations with a country, or (3) at the closure or opening of an embassy.

### Database Contents

The type of information included for each entry varies based on the type of position. Entries will have some or all of these pieces of information:

Name When possible, the full name of the appointee has been included.Years of birth and death State of residency The appointee’s state or territory of legal residence at the time of the appointment is taken from the commission, nomination, or a contemporary official record of legal residence. If the residence was omitted from these sources, the entry does not appear. Some officers changed their legal residence during their careers; in such cases multiple residences are listed.Career status (in the Foreign Service)The determination of which Chiefs of Mission were to be denominated as “career” officers posed a number of problems to the early compilers of this work, and continues to pose definitional challenges today. How early could Chief of Mission appointments be said to be of a career nature in view of the fact that until 1946 officers of the Diplomatic Service had to resign from the career services to accept appointment as Ambassador or Minister? Should an officer who had retired as a Foreign Service officer after a long career be considered a “career” officer when later appointed to an Ambassadorship? And what of an officer who had resigned from the Foreign Service after a brief career who was later appointed Chief of Mission? At the time the scope and format of this publication were being planned, a dozen such questions were submitted to the then-Director General of the Foreign Service. It was determined not to attempt to categorize Chiefs of Mission as “career” or “non-career” before the passage of the Act to Improve the Foreign Service on February 5, 1915 (38 Stat. 805), which restructured the Diplomatic and Consular Services. For Chiefs of Mission holding office as such at that date, it was decided to count as “career” those who had at least ten years of continuous diplomatic service under both Republican and Democratic administrations. For Chiefs of Mission appointed later, the term “career” was also applied to those who were at the time of appointment (or had previously been for at least five years) Foreign Service officers, Foreign Service information officers, or career officers in the Diplomatic or Consular Services. The term “career” was also applied to those few individuals who had served as diplomatic secretaries, who had then been commissioned before 1915 as Chiefs of Mission or as Presidential appointees in the Department of State, who were not serving as Chiefs of Mission in February 1915, but who were subsequently appointed or reappointed as such. The term “non-career” is used to designate all other appointees even though they may have been career officers in the civil or military services.Dates of service These dates are included on a position-by-position basis. Principal officers of the Department of State who are Presidential appointees have a date of appointment, date of entry on duty, and date of termination of appointment. Upon assuming charge of their mission, Chiefs of Mission possess the authority and responsibility to manage their post and oversee the conduct of its operations. Upon presenting their credentials to the host government, Chiefs of Mission are recognized as the principal diplomatic representative of the United States Government. Both assumption of charge over the U.S. mission and presentation of credentials to the host government are important elements of a Chief of Mission’s entrance on duty. As of 2019, “Assumed Charge” dates are tracked for Chiefs of Mission. An effort has been made to fix a date for the termination of the diplomatic mission of each representative vis-à-vis the host government and to describe briefly in each individual case (and as precisely as sometimes incomplete records permit) what action or event brought the mission to either a formal or a de facto close. In the nineteenth century it was customary for a Chief of Mission to present his own letter of recall; in current practice most missions terminate in actual fact with the departure of the Ambassador from his or her post. In all periods there have been special circumstances (e.g., death, declaration of war, severance of diplomatic relations) which have brought some diplomatic missions to an end. It should be emphasized that the effective date of a Chief of Mission’s resignation frequently does not coincide with the date shown here for the termination of his or her mission abroad. For those who were designated by the Secretary of State, the date of appointment is the same as the date of entry on duty. For Chargés d’Affaires ad interim, dates of service are listed from and to the nearest month.
### Key Terms

Appointment The date of appointment is that which appears upon the face of the Presidential commission issued to the appointee. It is frequently referred to as the date of commissioning or the date of attestation. Recess appointments are valid only until the end of the current session of the Senate. If the President wishes to keep a recess appointee in office, the President must re-nominate the appointee.Commission A document attesting that the appointee has been appointed as a principal officer of the Department of State or as a Chief of Mission. It is signed by the President and the Secretary of State and bears the impression of the Great Seal of the United States. “Commission” always connotes Presidential action.Designation This term covers chiefs of bureaus of the Department of State who are selected by the Secretary of State. Article II, Section 2 of the Constitution states that “the Congress may by law vest the Appointment of such inferior Officers, as they think proper, in the President alone, in the Courts of Law, or in the Heads of Departments.” “Designation” always connotes Secretarial action.Nomination This is the date that the President sends to the Senate the name of a person whom he wishes to appoint to a high-level position. Article II, Section 2 of the Constitution states that the President, “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the Supreme Court, and all other Officers of the United States, whose Appointments are not herein otherwise provided for, and which shall be established by Law.” Per[Senate Rule XXXI](https://www.rules.senate.gov/rules-of-the-senate), “Nominations neither confirmed nor rejected during the session at which they are made shall not be acted upon at any succeeding session without being again made to the Senate by the President; and if the Senate shall adjourn or take a recess for more than thirty days, all nominations pending and not finally acted upon at the time of taking such adjournment or recess shall be returned by the Secretary to the President, and shall not again be considered unless they shall again be made to the Senate by the President.”
### Steps in Appointment

Nomination is the first step in the appointment process. The President submits the name of the person to be appointed to a high-level position to the Senate for approval by first the Foreign Relations Committee and then by the full Senate. Approval by the full Senate is called “confirmation.” The appointee is then commissioned. After taking the oath of office, he or she enters on duty. Chiefs of Mission, however, are considered to have entered on duty when they present their credentials to their host governments.

The **United States ambassador to the United Kingdom**, formally the **ambassador of the United States of America to the Court of St James's**,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-WinfieldHouse-3) is the official representative of the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and the [United States government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_States "Government of the United States") to the [British monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_the_United_Kingdom "Monarchy of the United Kingdom") (the Court of St James's) and the [government of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-4) The position is currently held by [Warren Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens "Warren Stephens"), who presented his credentials to [King Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Charles_III "King Charles III") on May 21, 2025.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-Stephens_2025-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-The_Times_2025-2)

The position is regarded as one of the most prestigious posts in the [United States Foreign Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Foreign_Service "United States Foreign Service") due to the [Special Relationship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Relationship "Special Relationship") between the United States and the United Kingdom.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-5) The ambassadorship has been held by various notable politicians, including five who would later become president: [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams"), [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe"), [John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams "John Quincy Adams"), [Martin Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren "Martin Van Buren") and [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan"). However, the modern tendency of American presidents (of both parties) is to appoint keen political [fundraisers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundraisers "Fundraisers") from previous [presidential campaigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_campaign "Presidential campaign"), despite the importance and prestige of the office.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-6)

The [ambassador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador "Ambassador") and executive staff work at the [American Embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_London "Embassy of the United States, London") in [Nine Elms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Elms "Nine Elms"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). The official residence of the ambassador is [Winfield House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_House "Winfield House") in [Regent's Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent's_Park "Regent's Park").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-WinfieldHouse-3)

**Warren Amerine Stephens** (born February 18, 1957) is an American businessman who is the [United States ambassador to the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom "List of ambassadors of the United States to the United Kingdom") under President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") in his [second administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump"). He is the former chairman, president and chief executive officer (CEO) of [Stephens Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephens_Inc. "Stephens Inc."), a privately held [investment bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_bank "Investment bank").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-1)

On December 2, 2024, President-elect Trump announced his nomination of Stephens to serve as the ambassador to the United Kingdom. Stephens had donated $6 million to Trump prior to the nomination. The U.S. Senate confirmed his nomination in a 59–39 vote. He was sworn in on April 30, 2025, and presented his letters of credence on May 21, 2025.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Warren_Stephens&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Stephens was born in [Little Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Rock,_Arkansas "Little Rock, Arkansas"), the son of [Jackson T. Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_T._Stephens "Jackson T. Stephens") and Mary Amerine Stephens. Warren's father, "Jack" Stephens, and his uncle, "Witt" Stephens, partnered as investors and financiers in the investment firm, Stephens Inc.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-auto-2) His mother descends from Johann Hendrick Amrine, an orphan from 18th-century [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland") who was found floating in the [Rhine River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine_River "Rhine River") following a flood and subsequently named Amrine, "in the Rhine."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-4)

Warren began his education in Little Rock, and in 1975, graduated from [Trinity Presbyterian High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Presbyterian_School "Trinity Presbyterian School") in [Montgomery, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery,_Alabama "Montgomery, Alabama"). He graduated from [Washington and Lee University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_and_Lee_University "Washington and Lee University") in 1979 with a BA in economics, and received his MBA from [Wake Forest University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Forest_University "Wake Forest University") in 1981.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-auto1-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Warren_Stephens&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Stephens joined his father and uncle in the investment banking business in Little Rock, which had 139 employees. At that time, the firm resembled and operated much like one of the old British merchant banks, investing the firm's and family funds in various businesses and ventures, and it still operates the same way today. Stephens Inc., is noted for handling the IPO of [Wal-Mart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wal-Mart "Wal-Mart") Stores in 1970.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-auto-2)

Stephens began work as an associate in the corporate finance department, concentrating on oil and gas. He became head of the department in 1983 and spent a lot of time on mergers and acquisitions. On February 18, 1986, Stephens was appointed president and CEO of Stephens Inc.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-auto-2)

In 1990, he was the senior advisor to [Tyson Foods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyson_Foods "Tyson Foods") in its acquisition of Holly Farms in a nine-month takeover battle.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-auto-2) He is only the third chairman, president and CEO in the firm's more than 90 years of operations since 1933.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-6)

In 2006, Stephens acquired 100 percent of the outstanding shares of Stephens Inc., from the other family members.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-auto-2)

Stephens is on the board of [Dillard's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dillard's "Dillard's").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-7)

In January 2025, Warren Stephens revealed his decision to step down from his role as CEO of Stephens Inc., to prepare to assume the position of [U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom "U.S. Ambassador to the United Kingdom") His sons, Miles and John Stephens, have been named co-CEOs, representing the third generation of family leadership at the firm.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-8)

## Political involvement and government service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Warren_Stephens&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Political involvement and government service")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Secretary_of_State_Marco_Rubio_swears_in_Ambassador_to_the_U.K._Warren_Stephens_%2854488379010%29.jpg/250px-Secretary_of_State_Marco_Rubio_swears_in_Ambassador_to_the_U.K._Warren_Stephens_%2854488379010%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Secretary_of_State_Marco_Rubio_swears_in_Ambassador_to_the_U.K._Warren_Stephens_(54488379010).jpg)

Stephens being sworn in as the United States ambassador to the United Kingdom, April 2025

A [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"), he supported [Bob Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dole "Bob Dole") in 1996, [Steve Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Forbes "Steve Forbes") in 1999, and has supported [Mike Huckabee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Huckabee "Mike Huckabee").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-nytimes-9) Stephens was a [bundler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundler_(campaigning) "Bundler (campaigning)") for [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney") in 2012.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-bundler-10) He has been critical of presidents [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") and [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-forbes-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-business-12)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-nytimes-9) During the 2020 presidential election, Stephens donated more than $3 million to super PACs supporting Trump. In the 2024 Republican presidential primaries, Stephens was a major financial backer of [Asa Hutchinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asa_Hutchinson "Asa Hutchinson") and [Nikki Haley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikki_Haley "Nikki Haley").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-14) During the 2024 presidential campaign, Stephens also contributed to [MAGA Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make_America_Great_Again_Inc. "Make America Great Again Inc."), a [super PAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_PAC "Super PAC") that supported [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), donating a further $1 million during the first half of 2025.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-:1-16)

Stephens has been listed as the largest single donor to the Trump 2025 inauguration, gifting four million dollars, twice the amount of the three next largest donors. From 1989 to 2024, the investment banker contributed more than 77-million dollars to Republican candidates, 111 thousand to Democrat or Liberal candidates.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-17)

On December 2, 2024, President-elect Donald Trump announced his intent to nominate Stephens to serve as the [United States ambassador to the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom "List of ambassadors of the United States to the United Kingdom") in his second administration.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-18) At the time, Stephens had donated $6 million to Trump.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-19) On February 12, 2025, his nomination was sent to the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-20) His nomination was confirmed with a vote of 59–39 on April 29, 2025.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-:0-21) He [presented his credentials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_of_credence "Letter of credence") to [King Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Charles_III "King Charles III") on May 21, 2025, at Buckingham Palace.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-22) In June 2026, he appeared at the [American Museum and Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Museum_and_Gardens "American Museum and Gardens") in [Bath, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_England "Bath, England") to commemorate the [United States Semiquincentennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Semiquincentennial "United States Semiquincentennial").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-23)

## Philanthropy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Warren_Stephens&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Philanthropy")]

Stephens was on the board of trustees of his alma mater, Washington and Lee University.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-auto1-5) Stephens and his wife Harriet are benefactors of various organizations, most notably the [Episcopal Collegiate School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Collegiate_School "Episcopal Collegiate School") and the [Arkansas Arts Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_Arts_Center "Arkansas Arts Center"), both in Little Rock.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-25)

## Leisure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Warren_Stephens&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Leisure")]

Stephens built The Alotian Club golf course, opening in 2004, and overlooking [Lake Maumelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Maumelle "Lake Maumelle") in Arkansas. The club was designed by [Tom Fazio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Fazio "Tom Fazio") and rated the #37 best course in the United States by [Golf Digest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_Digest "Golf Digest") in 2025.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens#cite_note-27) He contributed land and financing for the creation of minor-league baseball stadium [Dickey-Stephens Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickey-Stephens_Park "Dickey-Stephens Park") in [North Little Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Little_Rock "North Little Rock"), opened in 2007 and bearing his family's namesake.

The **United States ambassador to the United Kingdom**, formally the **ambassador of the United States of America to the Court of St James's**,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-WinfieldHouse-3) is the official representative of the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and the [United States government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_States "Government of the United States") to the [British monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_the_United_Kingdom "Monarchy of the United Kingdom") (the Court of St James's) and the [government of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-4) The position is currently held by [Warren Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens "Warren Stephens"), who presented his credentials to [King Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Charles_III "King Charles III") on May 21, 2025.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-Stephens_2025-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-The_Times_2025-2)

The position is regarded as one of the most prestigious posts in the [United States Foreign Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Foreign_Service "United States Foreign Service") due to the [Special Relationship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Relationship "Special Relationship") between the United States and the United Kingdom.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-5) The ambassadorship has been held by various notable politicians, including five who would later become president: [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams"), [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe"), [John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams "John Quincy Adams"), [Martin Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren "Martin Van Buren") and [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan"). However, the modern tendency of American presidents (of both parties) is to appoint keen political [fundraisers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundraisers "Fundraisers") from previous [presidential campaigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_campaign "Presidential campaign"), despite the importance and prestige of the office.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-6)

The [ambassador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador "Ambassador") and executive staff work at the [American Embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_London "Embassy of the United States, London") in [Nine Elms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Elms "Nine Elms"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). The official residence of the ambassador is [Winfield House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_House "Winfield House") in [Regent's Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent's_Park "Regent's Park").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-WinfieldHouse-3)

## Duties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Duties")]

The ambassador's main duty is to present U.S. policies to the [government of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom") and its people, as well as report British policies and views to the [federal government of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States"). The ambassador serves as a primary channel of communication between the two nations and plays an important role in treaty negotiations.

The ambassador is the head of the United States' consular service in the United Kingdom. As well as directing diplomatic activity in support of trade, the ambassador is ultimately responsible for visa services and for the provision of consular support to American citizens in the UK and oversees cultural relations between the two countries.

### Ministers (1815–1893)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Ministers (1815–1893)")]

Diplomatic relations with what had now become the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland were restored after the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812"). The [Congress of Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_Vienna "Congress of Vienna") (1815) established a uniform system of [diplomatic rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_rank "Diplomatic rank"). Under that system, the highest rank of "ambassador" was a personal representative of a sovereign, and the next rank of "minister", represented a government. As a republic, the United States maintained diplomatic relations with Britain at the rank of _Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary_. The rank was colloquially known as _Minister_, and the position continued to be referred to as "United States Minister to Great Britain".

### Ambassadors (1893–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Ambassadors (1893–present)")]

Although France [became a republic in 1870](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Third_Republic "French Third Republic"), the country continued to exchange ambassadors with other Great Powers. In 1893, the United States followed the French precedent and upgraded its relations with other Great Powers to the ambassadorial level. The United States [Legation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legation "Legation") in London became the [United States Embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_London "Embassy of the United States, London"), and the United States Minister to Great Britain became the United States Ambassador to Great Britain.

**Warren Albert Stevens** (November 2, 1919 – March 27, 2012) was an American stage, screen, and television actor.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stevens#cite_note-nytimes-1)

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Warren_Stevens&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Stevens was born in [Clarks Summit, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarks_Summit,_Pennsylvania "Clarks Summit, Pennsylvania") and graduated from Clarks Summit High School.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stevens#cite_note-engaged-2) He attended the [Naval Academy Preparatory School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Academy_Preparatory_School "Naval Academy Preparatory School") and entered the [United States Naval Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Academy "United States Naval Academy") in 1937 but was medically discharged in 1940.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stevens#cite_note-engaged-2) In January 1942, he enlisted in the [United States Army Air Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Air_Forces "United States Army Air Forces") and became an aviation cadet.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stevens#cite_note-engaged-2) During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), he served in the Army Air Forces as a pilot.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

A founding member of the [Actors Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actors_Studio "Actors Studio") in New York,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stevens#cite_note-3) Stevens received notice on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") in the late 1940s, and thereafter was offered a Hollywood contract at [20th Century Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Fox "20th Century Fox"). His first Broadway role was in _[The Life of Galileo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Life\_of\_Galileo "The Life of Galileo")_ (1947)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stevens#cite_note-4) and his first movie role followed in _[The Frogmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Frogmen "The Frogmen")_ (1951). As a young studio contract player, Stevens had little choice of material, and he appeared in films that included _[Phone Call from a Stranger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phone\_Call\_from\_a\_Stranger "Phone Call from a Stranger")_ (1952), _[Wait Till the Sun Shines, Nellie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wait\_Till\_the\_Sun\_Shines,\_Nellie\_(film) "Wait Till the Sun Shines, Nellie (film)")_ (1952), and _[Gorilla at Large](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorilla\_at\_Large "Gorilla at Large")_ (1954). A memorable movie role was that of the ill-fated "Doc" Ostrow in the science fiction film _[Forbidden Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden\_Planet "Forbidden Planet")_ (1956). He also had supporting roles in _[The Barefoot Contessa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Barefoot\_Contessa "The Barefoot Contessa")_ (1954) with [Humphrey Bogart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey_Bogart "Humphrey Bogart") and _[Intent to Kill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intent\_to\_Kill\_(1958\_film) "Intent to Kill (1958 film)")_ (1958).

Despite occasional parts in big films, Stevens was unable to break out consistently into A-list movies, so he carved out a career in television as a journeyman dramatic actor.

## Television career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Warren_Stevens&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Television career")]

He co-starred as Lieutenant William Storm in _[Tales of the 77th Bengal Lancers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_of\_the\_77th\_Bengal\_Lancers "Tales of the 77th Bengal Lancers")_ ([NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC"), 1956–1957), a prime time adventure series set in India. Stevens also provided the voice of John Bracken in season one of _[Bracken's World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracken's\_World "Bracken's World")_ (NBC, 1968–1970). He played the role of Elliot Carson in the daytime series _[Return to Peyton Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return\_to\_Peyton\_Place\_(TV\_series) "Return to Peyton Place (TV series)")_ during its two-year run (1972–1974).

Stevens' appearance in the 1955 movie _[Robbers' Roost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbers'\_Roost\_(1955\_film) "Robbers' Roost (1955 film)")_ introduced him to [Richard Boone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Boone "Richard Boone"), who hired him for a continuing television role on _[The Richard Boone Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Richard\_Boone\_Show "The Richard Boone Show")_, an award-winning NBC anthology series which lasted for the 1963–1964 season.

Stevens was a close friend of actor [Richard Basehart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Basehart "Richard Basehart") and helped him through a difficult divorce in the early 1960s. Stevens guest-starred in a few episodes of Basehart's [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") series, _[Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyage\_to\_the\_Bottom\_of\_the\_Sea\_(TV\_series) "Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (TV series)")_. He also had a supporting role on another [Irwin Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irwin_Allen "Irwin Allen") production, _[The Return of Captain Nemo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Return\_of\_Captain\_Nemo "The Return of Captain Nemo")_ in 1978.

In his later years, Stevens' appearances were infrequent. He guest-starred in _[ER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ER\_(TV\_series) "ER (TV series)")_ in March 2006 and had two roles in 2007.

For the DVD release of _[Combat!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat! "Combat!")_ he provided [audio commentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_commentary "Audio commentary") for "The Gun" (S5, E1) an episode in which he had guest-starred. He also guest-starred in "The Imposter" (S3, E10).

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Warren_Stevens&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Death")]

Stevens died on March 27, 2012, from complications of lung disease in his home in [Sherman Oaks, Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman_Oaks,_Los_Angeles "Sherman Oaks, Los Angeles"), California. He had three children.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stevens#cite_note-5)

The **United States ambassador to the United Kingdom**, formally the **ambassador of the United States of America to the Court of St James's**,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-WinfieldHouse-3) is the official representative of the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and the [United States government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_States "Government of the United States") to the [British monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_the_United_Kingdom "Monarchy of the United Kingdom") (the Court of St James's) and the [government of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-4) The position is currently held by [Warren Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Stephens "Warren Stephens"), who presented his credentials to [King Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Charles_III "King Charles III") on May 21, 2025.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-Stephens_2025-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-The_Times_2025-2)

The position is regarded as one of the most prestigious posts in the [United States Foreign Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Foreign_Service "United States Foreign Service") due to the [Special Relationship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Relationship "Special Relationship") between the United States and the United Kingdom.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-5) The ambassadorship has been held by various notable politicians, including five who would later become president: [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams"), [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe"), [John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams "John Quincy Adams"), [Martin Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren "Martin Van Buren") and [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan"). However, the modern tendency of American presidents (of both parties) is to appoint keen political [fundraisers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundraisers "Fundraisers") from previous [presidential campaigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_campaign "Presidential campaign"), despite the importance and prestige of the office.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-6)

The [ambassador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador "Ambassador") and executive staff work at the [American Embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_London "Embassy of the United States, London") in [Nine Elms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Elms "Nine Elms"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). The official residence of the ambassador is [Winfield House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_House "Winfield House") in [Regent's Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent's_Park "Regent's Park").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-WinfieldHouse-3)

## Duties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Duties")]

The ambassador's main duty is to present U.S. policies to the [government of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom") and its people, as well as report British policies and views to the [federal government of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States"). The ambassador serves as a primary channel of communication between the two nations and plays an important role in treaty negotiations.

The ambassador is the head of the United States' consular service in the United Kingdom. As well as directing diplomatic activity in support of trade, the ambassador is ultimately responsible for visa services and for the provision of consular support to American citizens in the UK and oversees cultural relations between the two countries.

### Ministers (1815–1893)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Ministers (1815–1893)")]

Diplomatic relations with what had now become the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland were restored after the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812"). The [Congress of Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_Vienna "Congress of Vienna") (1815) established a uniform system of [diplomatic rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_rank "Diplomatic rank"). Under that system, the highest rank of "ambassador" was a personal representative of a sovereign, and the next rank of "minister", represented a government. As a republic, the United States maintained diplomatic relations with Britain at the rank of _Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary_. The rank was colloquially known as _Minister_, and the position continued to be referred to as "United States Minister to Great Britain".

### Ambassadors (1893–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_the_United_Kingdom&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Ambassadors (1893–present)")]

Although France [became a republic in 1870](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Third_Republic "French Third Republic"), the country continued to exchange ambassadors with other Great Powers. In 1893, the United States followed the French precedent and upgraded its relations with other Great Powers to the ambassadorial level. The United States [Legation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legation "Legation") in London became the [United States Embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_London "Embassy of the United States, London"), and the United States Minister to Great Britain became the United States Ambassador to Great Britain.

**Francis Lodowic Bartels** (13 March 1910 – 20 March 2010) was a [Ghanaian](link_5) diplomat and educationalist, who served as Ghana's ambassador to [West Germany](link_6) between 1970 and 1972.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Lodowic_Bartels#cite_note-africansuccess.org-1)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Francis_Lodowic_Bartels&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Francis Bartels was born in [Cape Coast](link_8) to the Rev. Charles Henry Bartels (1885–1938), a [Methodist](link_14) minister, and Agnes Mensah (1887–1940). He stems from a prominent [Gold Coast Euro-African](link_15) family from [Elmina](link_16). [Carel Hendrik Bartels](link_17) was his great-great-grandfather. One of his daughters is the Ghanaian diplomat, [Agnes Aggrey-Orleans](link_13).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Lodowic_Bartels#cite_note-2)

Bartels attended the [Mfantsipim School](link_18) between 1925 and 1928 and the [Wesley College of Education, Kumasi](link_19) between 1929 and 1931. A King Edward VII Scholarship allowed him to continue his studies at [King's College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King [link_20]'s_College_London "King's College London"), where he graduated in 1935 with a [Bachelor of Arts](link_21). He then returned to the Gold Coast to teach at the [Mfantsipim School](link_18). Between 1946 and 1947, Bartels studied teaching at the [University College London](link_22) and subsequently taught at the [Selly Oak Colleges](link_23) in [Birmingham](link_24). After he received a Master of Arts there, Bartels again returned to the Gold Coast, to become the first [Euro-African](link_15) President of the Mfantsipim School.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Lodowic_Bartels#cite_note-africansuccess.org-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Lodowic_Bartels#cite_note-3) From 1949-1961 he was the first black African headmaster of Mfantsipim School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Lodowic_Bartels#cite_note-4) He co-founded the Conference of Heads of Assisted Secondary Schools (CHASS) in the 1950s. CHASS is a platform for principals and heads of secondary schools in Ghana to discuss and exchange ideas and experiences regarding the administration of secondary education at the time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Lodowic_Bartels#cite_note-5)

In 1989 he was awarded an honorary doctorate in law (LL.D.) from the [University of Ghana](link_25).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Lodowic_Bartels#cite_note-6) He was a founding member of the Mfantsipim Lodge of the [District Grand Lodge of Ghana](link_26).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Lodowic_Bartels#cite_note-7)

He died in Paris a week after his 100th birthday.

# John Powell Jones

## Diplomat who was scrupulous in his duties which took him to war-torn Cambodia as well as Colombia, the Congo and Switzerland

![Image 2: 103131368_POWELL-JONES](https://cms.thetimes.com/wp-content/uploads/image-server/production/bade779c-2771-356a-a338-4566127e2b74.jpg?crop=0px%2C0px%2C1024px%2C683px)

Friday March 02 2012, 12.01am GMT, The Times

John Powell-Jones spent his life representing Britain abroad, often in difficult or dangerous places — Colombia in 1949, the Congo immediately after independence, Cambodia in the terminal stages of civil war — before ending his career as the UK’s representative at the Conference on the Law of the Sea and Ambassador to Switzerland.

John Ernest Powell-Jones was born in 1925 and educated at Charterhouse. He was one of a group of gifted pupils much influenced by the young headmaster Robert Birley under whose tutelage he won a scholarship to University College, Oxford. Before taking it up he served with the Rifle Brigade from 1943 to 1946, latterly as a lieutenant in Palestine. At Oxford he won first-class honours in modern history and two university prizes, and entered the Foreign Service in 1949.

## Diplomat who was scrupulous in his duties which took him to war-torn Cambodia as well as Colombia, the Congo and Switzerland

John Powell-Jones spent his life representing Britain abroad, often in difficult or dangerous places — Colombia in 1949, the Congo immediately after independence, Cambodia in the terminal stages of civil war — before ending his career as the UK’s representative at the Conference on the Law of the Sea and Ambassador to Switzerland.

John Ernest Powell-Jones was born in 1925 and educated at Charterhouse. He was one of a group of gifted pupils much influenced by the young headmaster Robert Birley under whose tutelage he won a scholarship to University College, Oxford. Before taking it up he served with the Rifle Brigade from 1943 to 1946, latterly as a lieutenant in Palestine. At Oxford he won first-class honours in modern history and two university prizes, and entered the Foreign Service in 1949.
